hooks.text: To explore the Sun's poles, a probe flew to Jupiter.
Why fly to Jupiter just to reach the Sun's poles?
A spacecraft flew 500 million miles away to visit the Sun.

title: The Probe That Flew to Jupiter to Reach the Sun
description: How NASA and ESA sent the Ulysses probe on a 500 million mile detour to orbit the Sun's poles.

beats.text: To explore the Sun's poles, a probe flew to Jupiter.
beats.visual: Illustration of Ulysses spacecraft flying near the Sun's polar regions, 1994

beats.text: Earth rockets lacked the power to turn straight up into solar orbit.
beats.visual: Diagram showing trajectory of Ulysses out of ecliptic plane via Jupiter, 1992
queries: Ulysses out of ecliptic orbit diagram

beats.text: So NASA and ESA launched Ulysses aboard Space Shuttle Discovery in 1990.
beats.visual: Photograph of Space Shuttle Discovery launching STS-41 carrying Ulysses, 1990

beats.text: Instead of heading inward, the probe raced straight toward giant Jupiter.
beats.visual: Hubble view of Jupiter full disk atmosphere, 1992

beats.text: Jupiter's powerful gravity hurled Ulysses 80 degrees off the solar plane.
beats.visual: Illustration of Ulysses executing Jupiter gravity assist maneuver, 1992

beats.text: The slingshot made Ulysses the fastest human object made up to 1990.
beats.visual: Cleanroom photograph of Ulysses probe undergoing assembly testing at ESA, 1989

beats.text: Above the poles, it discovered interstellar dust 30 times thicker than assumed.
beats.visual: SOHO satellite telescope photo of solar corona and dust, 1996

beats.text: To reach the top of our star, you must first fly away from it.
beats.visual: Solar Dynamics Observatory view of the Sun's polar magnetic regions, 2011
queries: Sun polar magnetic fields SDO image

better_than_last: Applied the proven rule of explaining orbital mechanics directly with clear visual comparisons without historical detours to maximize mid-video retention.
